The card lists one (id, source, target) tuple per edge, from (1, 1, 2) for edge 1 between A and B to (5, 3, 4) for edge 5 between C and D." width="100%"} Returns all edges in the graph as tuples containing the edge ID and the source and target node IDs. Useful for iterating over all edges or analyzing edge structure. This is the most direct way to get the full edge list in one call: unlike `get_edge_ids()`, there is no limit, and unlike calling `get_node_ids_by_edge_id()` per edge, the endpoints come along for free. That makes it a good starting point for: - looping over every edge, e.g. to compute something per edge or export an edge list - building adjacency structures or feeding the edges to another library - checking which node pairs are joined, including self-loops and parallel edges (each parallel edge appears as its own tuple) Tuples follow the graph's internal edge storage, which in practice is the order in which edges were added. In a directed graph `source` and `target` give the edge's direction; in an undirected graph they record the order in which the endpoints were given to `add_edge()`. All values are integer IDs, so translate node IDs with `get_label_from_id()` when you need labels, or use `get_edges_str_repr()` for a readable `"A->B"` form. Edge weights and attributes are not included; see `get_edge()` or `get_edge_df()` for those. Every edge is returned regardless of any selection. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of tuples where each tuple is `(edge_id, source_id, target_id)`. Empty if the graph has no edges. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Each tuple holds `(edge_id, source_id, target_id)`, giving direct access to an edge's endpoints without a separate lookup per edge: ::: {#ac119d42 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "C")]) ) graph.get_edges_as_tuples() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(1, 1, 2), (2, 1, 3), (3, 2, 3), (4, 3, 3)] ``` ::: ::: Unpacking the tuples makes it easy to build a readable edge list. The self-loop on `"C"` shows up with the same node as source and target: ::: {#0ca1f60b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} [ (eid, graph.get_label_from_id(src), graph.get_label_from_id(tgt)) for eid, src, tgt in graph.get_edges_as_tuples() ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [(1, 'A', 'B'), (2, 'A', 'C'), (3, 'B', 'C'), (4, 'C', 'C')] ``` ::: ::: The tuples also make simple per-node tallies straightforward, such as counting how many edges leave each node (`"A"` has two, `"B"` and `"C"` one each): ::: {#01bb436e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from collections import Counter Counter(graph.get_label_from_id(src) for _, src, _ in graph.get_edges_as_tuples()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` Counter({'A': 2, 'B': 1, 'C': 1}) ``` ::: :::
